clinical_knowledge.topic: Decompensated Heart Failure evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Decompensated Heart Failure is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes escalating diuretic therapy, strict fluid and sodium restriction, daily weight monitoring, and checking renal function and electrolytes, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: swollen ankles and shortness of breath for 3 weeks
Key HPI features: bilateral pitting oedema to mid-shin, orthopnoea (3 pillows), PND, dyspnoea on minimal exertion (walking 20 metres), no chest pain
Objective/Exam findings: Likely fluid overload. Requires weight, JVP, lung auscultation, BNP, renal function, ECG.
Relevant background/PMH: heart failure (EF 35%, diagnosed 2 years ago), atrial fibrillation, hypertension
Current medications: furosemide 40mg OD, bisoprolol 5mg OD, ramipril 5mg OD, warfarin (INR target 2-3)
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Decompensated Heart Failure.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Chronic kidney disease without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Breathlessness at rest, or waking at night gasping for air.
management_principles: Increase furosemide, strict fluid and sodium restriction, weigh daily, check renal function and electrolytes, consider cardiology review
Assess clinical stability, monitor vital parameters, and perform targeted diagnostic investigations.
Implement targeted therapeutic interventions per evidence-based clinical practice guidelines.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 72F with known HFrEF presents with 3-week worsening bilateral ankle oedema, orthopnoea (3 pillows), PND, and markedly reduced exercise tolerance. No chest pain.
reference_soap.objective: Likely fluid overload. Requires weight, JVP, lung auscultation, BNP, renal function, ECG.
reference_soap.assessment: Decompensated heart failure. DDx: medication non-compliance, dietary Na excess, worsening AF rate control, renal deterioration, new ischaemic event.
reference_soap.plan: Increase furosemide, strict fluid and sodium restriction, weigh daily, check renal function and electrolytes, consider cardiology review. Assess compliance.

learning_objectives: Systematically elicit heart failure symptoms (oedema, orthopnoea, PND, dyspnoea)
Review medication compliance and dietary history

teaching.one_liner: A weak heart cannot clear fluid, so it backs up into the legs and lungs — ankle swelling plus breathlessness is the classic pair.
red_flags: Breathlessness at rest, or waking at night gasping for air

must_ask.say: Do you get short of breath when you lie flat? How many pillows do you sleep on?
Do you ever wake up in the night suddenly gasping for breath?

must_ask.objective: Swelling — where and how far up
must_ask.say: Where does the swelling start, and how far up your legs does it go?
Have you put on weight recently, and how far can you walk before stopping?
Are you taking your water tablets exactly as prescribed?
How much salt do you use, and how much do you drink in a day?

history.answer: My ankles have been swelling up and I have been having a hard time catching my breath for about three weeks now.
It started around both ankles about three weeks ago, and now the swelling has worked its way halfway up both shins.
It started slowly over the past three weeks and has been steadily getting worse as the days go by.
My legs are swollen all day, but they definitely look much puffier in the evening after I have been up and about.
Yes, when I push on my shins my thumb leaves deep dents that take a while to go away, and my socks leave deep grooves.
I weighed myself two days ago and saw that I have gained about three kilograms over the last few weeks even though I am not eating more.
No, neither leg is red, warm, or painful, and I do not have any cramps in my calves.
I get winded very quickly now. Even walking twenty meters across my living room leaves me panting.
I cannot breathe comfortably lying flat anymore, so I have had to prop myself up on three pillows to sleep.
Yes, several times recently I woke up in the middle of the night gasping for air and had to sit right up by the window.
No, I have not had any chest pain, tightness, or pressure.
I have a dry cough that gets worse when I lie down, but I am not coughing up any phlegm or blood.
I have not noticed any frothy or dark cola-colored urine, but I feel like I am passing less water than usual.
My stomach has felt a little full and bloated recently, but it is not swollen or painful.
No, my eyes and skin are not yellow, and I have not had any unusual bruising or bleeding.
No, I have had no fever, chills, sore throat, or skin sores at all.
I do feel tired and worn out from waking up short of breath, but I am not sensitive to cold, and my skin is not dry.
My appetite is a little lower because of the bloated feeling, but I have not had chronic diarrhea or unintentional weight loss.
No, I have not been on any long flights or car trips, and I have not had any recent operations or bed rest.
I try to take all my pills, but I did miss a few doses of my water tablet over the past two weeks when I went out.
My daughter brought me some canned soups and pickled foods recently which were quite salty, and I have been drinking a lot of water.
I think my old heart condition is acting up again, just like when my heart pump was weak before.
I am really terrified that I might end up in the hospital again like I did last year.
I was hoping the doctor could check my water tablets and maybe adjust the strength so I can breathe better.
I was diagnosed with heart failure two years ago with thirty-five percent pump function, and I also have high blood pressure and atrial fibrillation.
I was admitted to the hospital for fluid buildup in my lungs about a year ago, but I have never had any surgery.
I take furosemide forty milligrams, bisoprolol five milligrams, ramipril five milligrams, and warfarin once a day.
No, I do not take any over-the-counter painkillers like ibuprofen, and I do not use steroids or herbal supplements.
I do not have any known allergies to medicines or foods.
I have never smoked cigarettes.
I do not drink any alcohol, and I have never had hepatitis or liver trouble.
I live alone in a single-story house, but my daughter lives nearby and visits me every day to help out.
My father died of a heart attack in his seventies, but there is no other early heart disease or kidney trouble in my family.

No periorbital edema is observed, and extraocular movements are intact.
Thyroid gland is normal in size, non-tender, and smooth without palpable nodules.
Jugular venous pressure is elevated at 4 cm above the sternal angle at 45 degrees, with positive hepatojugular reflux.
Heart rhythm is irregularly irregular with normal S1 and S2, and a soft S3 gallop is audible at the apex without murmurs.
Bilateral fine inspiratory crackles are heard over both lung bases extending up to the mid-lung zones.
Abdomen is mildly full but non-distended, with no visible collateral veins or scars.
Abdomen is soft and non-tender throughout without guarding or rebound tenderness.
Smooth liver edge is palpable 2 cm below the right costal margin without significant tenderness; spleen is not palpable.
Percussion note is tympanitic throughout the abdomen; shifting dullness and fluid wave are negative.
Bilateral symmetric 2+ pitting edema extends from both ankles up to the mid-shin level.
Calves are symmetric in circumference, soft, and non-tender bilaterally without erythema, warmth, or palpable cords.
